title: "The geometric distribution"

The CMUdict sequence introduced pronunciation entries and their phone counts. We now ask how many consonants precede the first vowel phone in each entry. This is a **waiting count**: the number of failures before the first success.

## Definition

If independent trials have constant success probability $p$, then

$$
X\sim\operatorname{Geometric}(p)
$$

has mass

$$
\mathbb{P}(X=x)=(1-p)^x p,
\qquad x\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\}.
$$

Differentiating the geometric series or using its probability-generating function gives

$$
\mathbb{E}[X]=\frac{1-p}{p},
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}[X]=\frac{1-p}{p^2}.
$$

To derive the mean, put $q=1-p$ and differentiate the geometric series: <!-- dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation -->

$$
\sum_{x=0}^{\infty}q^x=\frac{1}{1-q},
\qquad
\sum_{x=1}^{\infty}xq^{x-1}=\frac{1}{(1-q)^2}.
$$

Thus

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[X]
&=p\sum_{x=0}^{\infty}xq^x\\
&=pq\sum_{x=1}^{\infty}xq^{x-1}\\
&=\frac{1-p}{p}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The factorial moment $\mathbb{E}[X(X-1)]=2(1-p)^2/p^2$ then gives <!-- dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation -->

$$
\operatorname{Var}[X]
=\mathbb{E}[X(X-1)]+\mathbb{E}[X]-\mathbb{E}[X]^2
=\frac{1-p}{p^2}.
$$

The tail probability also has a simple form:

$$
\mathbb{P}(X\geq k)=(1-p)^k.
$$

## Fitting the CMUdict waiting count

Each CMUdict row is a dictionary pronunciation entry, not a running-speech token. The [earlier introduction](why-random-variables.qmd) links the 0.7b release and states the dependence among alternate pronunciations.

```{r}
#| label: fit-cmudict-geometric
library(ggplot2)

cmu <- read.csv(
  "data/cmudict/cmudict-pronunciations.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  na.strings = ""
)
wait <- cmu$consonants_before_first_vowel
p_hat <- 1 / (mean(wait) + 1) # dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation

fit <- data.frame(wait = 0:max(wait))
observed <- table(wait)
fit$observed_probability <- as.numeric(observed[as.character(fit$wait)]) / length(wait)
fit$fitted_probability <- dgeom(fit$wait, prob = p_hat)

empirical_variance <- mean((wait - mean(wait))^2)
fitted_variance <- (1 - p_hat) / p_hat^2

stopifnot(
  length(wait) == 133854L,
  !anyNA(wait),
  abs(sum(fit$observed_probability) - 1) < 1e-12,
  abs((1 - p_hat) / p_hat - mean(wait)) < 1e-12
)

data.frame(p_hat, empirical_mean = mean(wait), empirical_variance,
           fitted_mean = (1 - p_hat) / p_hat, fitted_variance)
```

The maximum-likelihood estimate is $\widehat p=1/(1+\overline X)$, computed as `r sprintf("%.3f", p_hat)`. The fitted mean thus matches the empirical mean. But the fitted variance is `r sprintf("%.3f", fitted_variance)`, while the empirical population variance is only `r sprintf("%.3f", empirical_variance)`.

```{r}
#| label: plot-cmudict-geometric
#| fig-cap: "Observed consonant waiting-count mass and fitted geometric mass. The fitted family matches the mean but greatly overstates the spread."
ggplot(fit, aes(wait)) +
  geom_col(aes(y = observed_probability), fill = "grey72", width = 0.8) +
  geom_line(aes(y = fitted_probability), color = "#8B1A1A", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(aes(y = fitted_probability), color = "#8B1A1A", size = 1.8) +
  labs(x = "Consonants before the first vowel", y = "Probability") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

## Why the fit fails

The geometric process assumes independent phone positions with one constant vowel probability. English phonotactics, syllable structure, and the dictionary's lexical composition violate that process story. Matching a mean is thus not evidence that the family explains the observed shape.

## Check your understanding

1. Compare the observed and fitted probabilities at the empirical median waiting count.
2. Derive $\widehat p=1/(1+\overline X)$ from the geometric log likelihood.
3. Which aspect of the plot reveals underdispersion relative to the fitted family?
4. Why are pronunciation alternatives not independent word types?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. At the empirical median wait of 1, the observed probability is 0.698388 and the fitted geometric probability is 0.249993. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. Differentiating $\ell(p)=n\log p+(\sum_i x_i)\log(1-p)$ and setting the derivative to zero gives $n/p-\sum_i x_i/(1-p)=0$, hence $\widehat p=1/(1+\overline X)$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. The observed distribution is much more concentrated at wait 1, with variance 0.321470 versus the fitted 2.031825, which shows underdispersion relative to the geometric family. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Pronunciation alternatives are clustered within an orthographic word, so they are neither distinct word types nor independent lexical observations. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>

The [negative-binomial distribution](negative-binomial-distribution.qmd) generalizes the waiting count to a later success.
